title: Dorothy Day
hookLine: a journalist who starts the Catholic Worker, houses of hospitality for the poor

lines: A NEWSROOM THAT IS ALSO A KITCHEN.
cards: A pot of soup is on the stove in a cramped office in New York, and the line for it reaches out the door and down the block. The woman ladling it out used to write for radical newspapers.

She has marched with socialists, been arrested with suffragists, and lived the bohemian life of Greenwich Village. Now she's a Catholic, which surprised her old friends, and she still runs a newspaper.
Only this one is about the poor, and the office doubles as a kitchen. Anyone hungry can sit down.

teach.h: A CONVERT WHO KEPT HER CAUSES.
teach.b: Dorothy Day came into the Catholic Church as an adult and didn't leave her care for workers and the poor at the church door.

She met a French wanderer and thinker, Peter Maurin, who liked to recite his plan out loud: people should feed the hungry and shelter the homeless themselves, face to face, not hand it all to an agency.

teach.h: A PAPER, THEN HOUSES OF HOSPITALITY.
teach.b: Together they started a paper, The Catholic Worker, and then houses of hospitality, where people with nowhere else to go could eat and sleep. Farms followed.
The houses spread to other cities, run by volunteers who often lived in them. The plan came out of an old Christian list, the works of mercy.
Most of the first list is in Matthew, where Jesus describes the judgment of the nations.

teach.h: I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in." Naked and clothed, sick and visited, in prison and visited.
The old catechisms call these the corporal works of mercy, the body works, and add one from tradition: burying the dead.
A second list, the spiritual works, includes teaching, counseling, comforting, forgiving and praying. Day treated the lists as a job description.

She wrote and argued against war and for workers, and went to jail for her protests. She lived in the houses herself, poor among the poor. People who knew her call her fierce and impatient as well as kind.
She is remembered for brushing off the word saint, so nobody could use it to dismiss her work as too hard for ordinary people. The Catholic Church has since opened her cause for sainthood anyway.

how: Catholic Worker communities still run houses of hospitality and farms, where volunteers live alongside guests, share meals, and keep a daily rhythm of prayer and work. Some parishes also organize the works of mercy through food pantries, prison visits and funeral ministries.

games.q: you've become a Catholic and you want to help the poor. Peter Maurin says do it yourself, face to face. what do you start?
o: a fundraising office that sends money to agencies.
a paper, and a house where anyone hungry can come in.
a quiet life of private prayer, away from the city.
games.why: Day and Maurin started The Catholic Worker, then houses of hospitality, and lived in them alongside their guests.

practice: Where is your own door? A table, a couch, the seat beside you on the bus. Let one face come to mind who might need a place at it, a coworker eating alone, a neighbor without visitors, and one small welcome you could offer.
Day's houses started with a pot of soup.

wordCard.voice: Dorothy Day. A journalist who became a Catholic and, with Peter Maurin, started the Catholic Worker and its houses of hospitality.
